## Proof

**Answer: Yes, the power series belongs to $\mathbb{Q}[[z]]$.**

**Setup.** Let $f(z) = \sum_{n \geq 0} a_n z^n$ with $a_n \in \mathbb{Q}$. Define
$$F(z) := \sum_{i=1}^{s} b_i\, f(\alpha_i z).$$

Since $a_n \in \mathbb{Q} \subseteq K$ and $\alpha_i, b_i \in K$, each coefficient of $f(\alpha_i z)$ is $a_n \alpha_i^n \in K$, and so $F(z) \in K[[z]]$ with $n$-th coefficient $c_n = \sum_{i=1}^{s} b_i\, a_n\, \alpha_i^n \in K$.

**Galois action on $F$.** For $\sigma \in G$, the action of $\sigma$ on the coefficients of $F$ gives
$$\sigma(F)(z) = \sum_{n \geq 0} \sigma(c_n)\, z^n = \sum_{n \geq 0}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s} \sigma(b_i)\, a_n\, \sigma(\alpha_i)^n\right) z^n = \sum_{i=1}^{s} \sigma(b_i)\, f(\sigma(\alpha_i)\, z),$$
where we used that $\sigma$ fixes each $a_n \in \mathbb{Q}$. Thus the given product is precisely
$$\prod_{\sigma \in G} \sigma(F)(z) =: N(F)(z),$$
the **norm** of $F$ from $K[[z]]$ to $\mathbb{Q}[[z]]$.

**$N(F)$ is well-defined as a formal power series.** The product of finitely many formal power series over $K$ is again a formal power series over $K$; its coefficients are polynomial expressions (with $\mathbb{Z}$-coefficients) in the coefficients of the factors, hence lie in $K$. So $N(F) \in K[[z]]$.

**$G$-invariance.** For any $\tau \in G$, applying $\tau$ to the coefficients of $N(F)$:
$$\tau\!\left(\prod_{\sigma \in G} \sigma(F)\right) = \prod_{\sigma \in G} \tau\bigl(\sigma(F)\bigr) = \prod_{\sigma \in G} (\tau\sigma)(F) = \prod_{\rho \in G} \rho(F) = N(F),$$
since left-multiplication by $\tau$ permutes the group $G$. Therefore every coefficient of $N(F)$ is fixed by all $\tau \in G$.

**Conclusion.** Since $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois, the fixed field is $K^G = \mathbb{Q}$. Each coefficient of $N(F)$ lies in $K^G = \mathbb{Q}$, so
$$N(F)(z) = \prod_{\sigma \in G}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s} \sigma(b_i)\, f(\sigma(\alpha_i)\, z)\right) \in \mathbb{Q}[[z]]. \qquad \blacksquare$$
